claims.text: The as-synthesized Mg-containing alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy contains no intermetallic precipitates.
Service exposure transforms the metastable solid solution into a multiphase microstructure containing intermetallic compounds.
The intermetallic compounds formed during service may include Laves phases.
Differential diffusion, particularly involving Mg and other alloying elements, drives nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds from the supersaturated solid solution.
Moderate service exposure produces limited precipitation and a fine, dispersed intermetallic phase.
Prolonged or harsher exposure causes intermetallic precipitates to coarsen or agglomerate.
Fine intermetallic precipitates alter local chemistry and stress in a way that promotes a uniform, adherent protective oxide film.
A protective surface film can be associated with passivation and high corrosion resistance in an Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloy.
A fine, dispersed intermetallic phase maintains or slightly improves corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
A fine, dispersed intermetallic phase maintains or slightly improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Coarsened precipitates compromise the continuity of the protective oxide scale.
Loss of oxide-scale continuity causes reduced corrosion resistance.
Loss of oxide-scale continuity causes reduced high-temperature oxidation resistance.
There is a critical precipitate size or volume fraction below which the protective film remains continuous and above which it fails.
Exposure near 900 °C in air is a relevant high-temperature service regime for testing the proposed transformation.
Exposure to 3.5% NaCl solution is a relevant aggressive corrosion regime for testing the proposed mechanism.
The proposed mechanism predicts a correlation among precipitate coarsening, oxide-film disruption, and degradation of corrosion or oxidation performance.
